Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

vignette:
Rangi Taumata is a 67-year-old widowed Māori man who works as an interior designer in Portland, Oregon. He was referred for psychological assessment following a captivity experience that occurred approximately fourteen months ago, during which he was detained for several days by armed men while on a professional consultation trip abroad. His PCL-5 score of 57 places him firmly within the severe range, and what emerged across the intake and early sessions was a presentation shaped less by a single overwhelming moment than by the cumulative, grinding quality of those days - the small room, the concrete walls pressing close, the guards' voices rising and falling in Arabic just beyond a locked door, the absolute uncertainty about whether he would survive.

During the detention, Rangi was held in a room no larger than a storage closet. He was not physically harmed, but the shouting - unpredictable, sometimes directed at him through the door, sometimes distant - became the rhythm of his captivity. He could not see who was speaking or what they wanted. He learned to read the sound of voices as his only available signal of danger. By the time he was released, his nervous system had been trained by those days into a hair-trigger vigilance that did not switch off when the door finally opened.

In the months that followed, Rangi found that his memories of the event were fragmented and unreliable in ways that disturbed him deeply. Sometimes he could describe what happened with a strange detachment, as though recounting something that had happened to a man he had once read about - flat, affectless, almost clinical. At other times, attempting to explain what occurred to his daughter or his GP, he would lose the thread entirely, the sentence dissolving mid-thought, and he would sit in silence, unable to recover it. Most distressing were the moments when memory arrived with sound: the specific cadence of shouting in Arabic, heard internally with a clarity that made him check the room. These auditory intrusions carried with them an immediate surge of threat - fear, shame at his helplessness, a bodily alarm that preceded any conscious thought. His heart would be pounding before he had registered what triggered it, his body already scanning for exits while his mind was still catching up.

Because the memory itself arrived so charged with threat, and because that threat reactivated the sensory texture of the original experience, Rangi found himself caught in a loop he could not name but could feel. The sense of danger made the memories more vivid; the memories made the sense of danger feel more justified. He became certain, in a way that felt entirely rational to him, that strong emotion itself was a warning - that feeling afraid or ashamed meant something real was wrong, that his body knew things his mind hadn't processed yet.

This conviction shaped everything that followed. Before any social interaction - a call with a client, a conversation with his building's concierge - Rangi began rehearsing what he would say, running through scenarios to ensure nothing would catch him off guard. He stopped taking on projects that required site visits to construction zones or mechanical rooms, spaces where the walls came close and the exits weren't immediately visible. Over several months, he began avoiding his studio altogether on days when the threat felt high, telling clients he was unwell. His business, once a source of genuine pride, contracted noticeably. A long-standing collaboration with an architectural firm quietly ended when he failed to appear at three consecutive meetings. These strategies gave him short-term relief but kept him from testing the beliefs that drove them, and the world outside his apartment continued to feel like a place that required constant management. What he had not anticipated was that the avoidance itself was keeping the memory alive: because he had never stayed in a situation long enough for the experience to resolve, the trauma memory remained unprocessed and undisturbed, surfacing with the same raw immediacy it had carried on the first day - the suppression had not quieted it but preserved it, intact and charged, exactly where he had left it. The rehearsing and withdrawing left him less practiced at ordinary interaction, more alert to unpredictability, more certain that something would go wrong if he lowered his guard. The strategies themselves had sealed off any possibility of disconfirmation: never having remained in a threatening situation long enough to find it safe, his nervous system had never received the evidence it needed, and the very act of escaping or preparing had functioned as a daily confirmation that the danger was real and ongoing - the threat remained as high as the day it was set.

What finally brought Rangi to seek help was a morning in the supermarket when a man nearby began arguing loudly in Arabic on his phone. Rangi was at the back of the store. He left his cart in the aisle and walked out without buying anything, sat in his car for forty minutes, and drove home. It was the triggers themselves - the shouting voice, the confined spaces, the unpredictable sounds - that had been driving his strategies all along: each time one surfaced, he found himself retreating, rehearsing, or withdrawing before he had made any conscious decision to do so, as though avoidance were the only available response his body knew. He told the intake clinician that he had not left the apartment for the four days that followed. What he is most afraid of, he said quietly, is that this is simply who he is now. What he is hoping for - and he used the word carefully, as though it might not survive contact with reality - is to be able to work again.
